transcript: Ask a Gen Z kid why they'll spend $7 on a matcha but won't put that same money toward a house and they'll say it's just a treat, a little self care. He had it backwards because there's a name for what's actually happening. In 2001, the chairman of Estee Lauder noticed that in the depths of a recession, lipstick sales went up. He called it the lipstick effect. When the big purchase becomes impossible, people don't save the difference. They pour it into small luxuries that still feel like winning. Researchers confirmed the pattern in 2012 and the big purchase really is impossible. In 1985, a home costs three and a half times a year's income. Today it's over five, past 10 in San Francisco. Since 1980, house prices climbed 551%. Wages, 373%. If pay had kept pace with housing, the typical household would earn $115,000 a year. It earns $83,000. So run the math on the matcha. Quit it entirely, bank every cent, and you reach a down payment in about 38 years. By which point the house costs several times more. The matcha is $7. The gap is $32,000 a year. Here's what nobody says. The matcha isn't why they're broke. It's the only thing in the whole equation that actually pays off. The house gives them nothing today, maybe nothing ever. title: The peak-end rule: why people chose more pain
summary: In a cold-water experiment most people chose the longer, more painful option. The peak-end rule explains how memory judges experiences.
transcript: The people were once given a choice between less pain and more pain as most of them picked more. It was an experiment with painfully cold water. People held one hand in it for a minute and with the other hand they did a minute in the same cold water then they kept it in for 30 more seconds when the water got just a little less forth. So the second one was strictly worse because it was the same pain and then some more of it. Afterwards they were asked which one they'd rather do again and most of them chose the longer one. And why would anyone pick more pain? It's because memory really doesn't keep a running thought. What it holds on to most is the worst moment and the last one and the longer one ended in little bits. Researchers call this the peak end. It's why a trip with one terrible last day can feel like a bad trip even when most of it was amazing. I think this is worth remembering about anything in your life that's in your back. Maybe it's your college that ended with a fight with your friend or a job where the last one was awful. Your memory means really hard on the worst bit and on how it ended. But you lived all the middle parts too which were honestly maybe amazing and most of those years were good. So don't let the last 30 seconds tell you what the whole thing was ever in your life.

title: Why the Caspian Sea is actually a lake
summary: The Caspian is salty, huge and stormy, so why is it the world's largest lake and not a sea? It comes down to one missing link to the ocean.

But through the Vosporus, and a series of seas and straits, it reaches the Mediterranean, then passes through the Strait of Gibraltar into the Atlantic Ocean. title: The coastline paradox: how India's coast grew by 3,500 km
summary: India's official coastline jumped from about 7,500 km to over 11,000 km without the coast moving. The coastline paradox explains why.
transcript: There's something called the Coastline paradox and it's going to change the way you look at 2026. Hear me out. India's Coastline got about 3 and a half thousand kilometers longer recently and all anyone did was just measure it again. So how does the Coast get longer without moving at all? For decades the official number was about 7500 kilometers and from a measurement done around 1970. Then they measured again recently with much more detailed maps and it came out at over 11000. The Coast is exactly where it was so the only thing that changed is how closely they looked. And this is actually a famous puzzle called the Coastline paradox. If your ruler is 100 kilometers long you skip right over every bay and every rock but if your ruler is 1 kilometers long you go in and out of all of those little curves. So the number gets bigger. A British scientist ran into this while he was studying war. He wanted to know if countries with longer borders fought more wars. And he found that Spain and Portugal couldn't even agree on their own border. One said it was about 987 kilometers and the other said it was about more than 1200. It was the same border just measured with different rulers and the smaller your ruler gets the longer the coast gets because there's always a smaller curve to follow. Now think about the end of December this year. You're in bed late at night scrolling through everyone's year in review course and everybody seems to have had trips and promotions and you will feel like you probably did nothing this year. I think that's because we measure our own lives with a really big ruler. You look back and you can count maybe two or three big things but try a smaller ruler. Count every conversation where you help someone and every day you showed up when you didn't want to. That number would be enormous.
